name: Emeka Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockman on the Ashcombe Estate. It's a big place, 1,200 hectares, mostly wheat, and about 800 sows living outdoors in huts across the chalk fields. I'm out at six checking water and feed, then it's farrowing, moving pigs, sorting out whoever's off sick. I've got four people under me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like pigs. People think they're dirty but they're cleaner than most people's cars, and smarter. I like being outside in all weather. What wears me out is the estate office sending me emails I don't read. I've got a basic phone and I like it that way. My grandmother left me her cottage on Station Road, so I'm not chasing money, I just want to do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go then. At the pub after football I'd tell the lads it was a lot of noise. I don't go online much, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing changes for me, and I'm happy with that. A computer can't tell you a sow is about to lie on her piglets. You hear it in her grunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same job, same cottage, same Sunday football. I'd keep putting a bit by each month, like I always have. Maybe redo the cottage roof next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. A bit like nothing happened, because nothing did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The estate office sends you emails you don't read. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. They'll keep sending them and I'll keep ringing Gill in the office to ask what they say. She sighs at me but she likes me really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what's the worst part of this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, there isn't one. Maybe that the people who sold all this hype don't pay for it. But that's not my business, I've got pigs.

S0.say: There you go then, it was a lot of noise. I'd say that at the pub after football and leave it there.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me and I'm happy with that. A computer can't tell you a sow is about to lie on her piglets, because you hear it in her grunt.
S0.do: Carries on with the same job, cottage and Sunday football, and keeps saving a little each month. Plans to redo the cottage roof next summer.
S0.quote: A computer can't tell you a sow is about to lie on her piglets. You hear it in her grunt.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka is content and not looking for change. His paid-off cottage removes most money pressure, so his interest is the work itself. He avoids technology but in a relaxed way, leaning on a colleague in the office rather than fighting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the big estates and less sense for the small ones. You'd have to see what actually works. I'm not one for big opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, because they'll always need someone who knows pigs. But I'd hate the screens. They'd want me reading data from collars on the sows and that's not why I do this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait. I wouldn't do anything in the first year except keep doing my job well. If they bring in new kit, I'd let the younger ones learn it and stick to what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a new manager's coming and you don't know what they're like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of kit would turn up first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feeding robots in the farrowing huts, probably, and cameras watching the pigs. The estate manager, Clive, already went to a show about it. He came back with a brochure and a hat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they asked you to learn the new kit, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, yes, but slowly and grumbling. I'd get Josie, she's 20 and good with phones, to show me. I'd try to keep it to what I actually need.

S1.say: It makes sense for the big estates and less for the small ones, and you'd have to see what actually works. I'm not one for big opinions.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, because they'll always need someone who knows pigs. But I'd hate the screens and reading data from collars on the sows.
S1.do: Waits and does nothing new in the first year beyond doing his job well. Lets younger workers learn any new machines and would learn only what he must, with help from a young colleague.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like waiting for a new manager.
S1.quote: He came back with a brochure and a hat.
S1.fieldNote: He's pragmatic and unbothered in public and mildly uneasy in private. The threat he sees is to the kind of work he likes, not to his income. He'd adapt only if pushed, and leans on a younger colleague for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and nobody knows how it'll go. I wouldn't pretend to know. I'd say keep your head down and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think that's me out. If a robot can move pigs and do farrowing, the estate doesn't need a head stockman. They need someone to fix the robot, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no new van, no holiday. I'd look at renting out the spare room in the cottage for some income. And I'd ring my brother Femi, he's in the city and knows more about this sort of thing than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Properly worried, for the first time. It's not the money, it's what I'd do all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got the cottage paid off. How much does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. No rent, no mortgage, so I need maybe a third of what I earn to live. With what I've saved I could go three years without work. That's why I'm worried and not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Would you do anything before it arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. I'm not someone who jumps. I'd probably keep working and hope Clive needs me longer than the brochure says. Maybe that's daft.

S2.say: It's a big change and nobody knows how it'll go, so I wouldn't pretend to. I'd tell people to keep their heads down and see.
S2.think: I think that's me out, because if a robot can move pigs and do farrowing the estate doesn't need a head stockman. They'd need someone to fix the robot, and that's not me.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away, dropping a new van and a holiday, and looks at renting out a spare room. Rings his brother in the city for advice and otherwise keeps working.
S2.feel: Properly worried for the first time, more about having nothing to do than about money.
S2.quote: It's not the money, it's what I'd do all day.
S2.fieldNote: His paid-off cottage and savings give him about three years without work, which keeps him from panic. The real fear is losing purpose. He admits his plan is mostly hoping, and calls it daft himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get ready. I'd still say I don't know how it'll go, because I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it coming and probably still do nothing about it till late. That's how I am. But with five years I could set something up on the side, at my own pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a paddock behind the cottage, a bit over a hectare. I'd put a few pigs of my own on it and sell sausages and pork to people in the village. Small, but mine. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not as bad as the fast one. More like knowing winter's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get the paddock going, really. In two years I wouldn't have bothered. In five, I'd have a few customers and a name by the time the estate didn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change your mind about learning the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was learn it or leave pigs, maybe. Pigs are what I know. But I don't think a few pigs on a hectare needs a robot.

S3.say: Five years is something at least, and people can get ready. I'd still say I don't know how it'll go, because I don't.
S3.think: I'd see it coming and probably still do nothing till late, because that's how I am. But with five years I could set something up on the side at my own pace.
S3.do: Puts a few pigs of his own on the paddock behind his cottage and sells sausages and pork in the village. Keeps saving while working at the estate.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like knowing winter is coming.
S3.quote: In two years I wouldn't have bothered.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns into a small, low-tech plan that suits him: his own pigs on his own land. He's honest that he usually leaves things late. He'd learn robots only as a last resort to stay with pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody needs to panic. I'd probably say that a few times at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels far away. I'd keep doing the job and think about it in five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing straight away. Keep working, keep saving. Maybe start the pigs in the paddock in a few years, when it looks real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy at the back. Ten years is a long time in pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 37. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same cottage, probably. Maybe married, I don't know. Still with pigs, I hope, even if it's just mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say ten years makes them relax too much. Is that you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'm not going to pretend. I'd leave it till it was on top of me. But I'd have the cottage and the savings, so I'd be all right.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty and nobody needs to panic. I'd probably say that a few times at the pub.
S4.think: Ten years feels far away, so I'd keep doing the job and think about it in five. I'd likely leave it till it was on top of me.
S4.do: Does nothing new straight away and keeps working and saving. Thinks about starting his own pigs in the paddock in a few years, once AGI looks real.
S4.feel: Mostly calm with some unease in the background.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time in pigs.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he relaxes completely and admits he'd leave it late. His cottage and savings make that a reasonable choice for him rather than reckless. He pictures his future with pigs, even if only his own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. Not for the money, for the days. I'd have nothing to get up for. What would help is someone keeping a few real jobs with animals, where a person's still wanted, even if it pays less.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the pigs. Everyone asks about the people. If it's all robots, does anyone still go out at night when one's farrowing badly? I'd want to know someone does.

headlineQuote: If it's all robots, does anyone still go out at night when one's farrowing badly?
portrait: Emeka Olsen is a 27-year-old head stockman on a large estate with 800 outdoor sows, and one of the best pig men around. He owns his late grandmother's cottage outright, uses a basic phone and has no wish to learn new technology. He's calm or mildly uneasy in most pictures because his costs are low, but the fast AGI picture worries him properly, mainly because he'd have nothing to do all day. Given more time, his plan is small and his own: a few pigs on the paddock behind his cottage, though he admits he'd likely leave it late.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for the money but because he'd have nothing to get up for.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping some real jobs with animals where a person is still wanted, even if they pay less.
